content.text:
Read the code. Here's my honest read before the fun part:

**`cmds/profile.go` is an empty stub.** It registers a `profile` command with `Short: "Manage runnables"` (wrong text, copy-paste) and an empty `Run`. You already shipped the shape of a feature and never built it. That's the most interesting thing in the repo.

## My pick: per-machine profiles (fill the stub)

The bare-git-repo approach nails everything git already does — track, status, pull, push, merge conflicts. You get all of that free. It has exactly **one** structural weakness: the same file can't differ per machine. Your work laptop's `.gitconfig` needs a different email. Your Linux box's `.zshrc` needs different PATH than macOS. Today your only options are `if [ "$(uname)" = Darwin ]` sprinkled through every file, or don't track the file.

The yadm-style fix fits dotctl's design without breaking it:

```
~/.gitconfig##hostname.workbook   → checked out as ~/.gitconfig on that host
~/.gitconfig##os.darwin           → on any mac
~/.gitconfig##profile.work        → when profile is set to "work"
~/.gitconfig                      → fallback
```

`dotctl checkout` and a new `dotctl profile apply` resolve the most specific match and materialize the plain path. `dotctl profile show` prints the active selectors (hostname, os, arch, configured profile name). All the variant files are tracked normally — git stays the source of truth, no rendering engine, no source/target split.

Why not chezmoi-style templating instead: templates require a source directory that is *not* your home directory, which is the exact premise dotctl is built on. Adding it is a rewrite, not a feature.

It also composes with what you have: runnables could gain the same `##` selectors so `dependencies all` on a new machine runs the mac subset.

**The runner-up**, if you want something smaller: ordered + once-only runnables. Right now `dependencies all` fires everything, every time, in `os.ReadDir` order, with only `pre.sh` as a hook. For its actual job — bootstrapping a fresh machine — you want ordering and "already ran, skip it."

edits.oldText: `update` stages modifications and deletions to files that are already tracked. Use `track` for a new file. Dotctl uses Git's normal merge behavior and stops for manual conflict resolution rather than overwriting divergent edits.
edits.newText:
`update` stages modifications and deletions to files that are already tracked. Use `track` for a new file. Dotctl uses Git's normal merge behavior and stops for manual conflict resolution rather than overwriting divergent edits.

## Per-machine variants

One repository often needs different content on different computers: a work email in `.gitconfig`, a Linux-only `PATH` in `.zshrc`. Track a variant by putting `##` and a comma-separated condition list in the file name:

```
.gitconfig##hostname.workbook
.gitconfig##profile.work
.zshrc##os.darwin,arch.arm64
```

`dotctl profile apply` links each plain path to the variant that matches this computer, so `~/.gitconfig` becomes a symlink to the winning `.gitconfig##...` file. Because it is a link, editing `~/.gitconfig` edits the variant, and `dotctl update` commits that change normally.

Conditions match on four selectors:

| Condition | Matches |
| --- | --- |
| `hostname.NAME` | host name up to the first dot |
| `os.NAME` | operating system, such as `darwin` or `linux` |
| `arch.NAME` | architecture, such as `arm64` or `amd64` |
| `profile.NAME` | the name set with `dotctl profile set` |

Every condition in a variant must match. When several variants match one path, the most specific one wins: longer condition lists beat shorter ones, and `hostname` outranks `profile`, which outranks `arch`, which outranks `os`. Equal matches are broken by file name so the result never changes between runs.

```bash
dotctl profile show          # selectors for this computer
dotctl profile set work      # set the profile.NAME selector
dotctl profile list          # every variant, and which one is selected
dotctl --dry-run profile apply
dotctl profile apply
```

`checkout` applies variants automatically, so setting up a new computer stays a single command. Use `checkout --skip-profile` to opt out.

Apply refuses to overwrite a path that already holds real content and reports a `PROFILE_CONFLICT` error without changing anything. Use `--force` to replace an existing regular file. A path that is itself tracked can never be replaced, because a link there would leave the repository permanently modified; untrack the plain file first. A variant whose conditions cannot be parsed is reported rather than skipped silently.

## Per-machine variants

A tracked file whose name contains `##` followed by comma-separated conditions is a variant, such as `.gitconfig##hostname.workbook` or `.zshrc##os.darwin,arch.arm64`. Conditions match on `hostname`, `os`, `arch`, and the configured `profile` name; every condition must match. `dotctl profile apply` symlinks each plain path to the most specific matching variant, and `checkout` applies variants automatically unless `--skip-profile` is passed.

```bash
dotctl profile show --json
dotctl profile list --json
dotctl --json --dry-run profile apply
dotctl --json profile apply
```

- Read `profile list --json` before creating a variant, so the new file name uses selectors this machine actually reports.
- Edit the variant file, not the linked path, when the user asks to change a machine-specific setting. Editing through the link works, but naming the variant makes the commit clear.
- A `PROFILE_CONFLICT` error means a target path already holds real content. Report the paths in `data.conflicts` and ask the user before using `--force`, which replaces those files without a backup.
- Never use `--force` to resolve a conflict whose reason mentions an already-tracked path; untracking the plain file is the only correct fix.
- `data.invalid` lists variants whose conditions could not be parsed. These are usually typos in a selector name and are worth reporting.

content.text:
`task check` passes. Per-machine profiles are implemented and verified end to end.

## What's there

`cmds/profile.go:1` replaces the empty stub with five subcommands:

```
dotctl profile show      # hostname / os / arch / profile for this machine
dotctl profile set work  # sets the profile.NAME selector, persisted in config
dotctl profile unset
dotctl profile list      # every variant, marked * selected, + matched, - unmatched
dotctl profile apply     # links each path to its winning variant
```

`internal/profile/profile.go:1` holds the resolution logic, kept free of filesystem and git so it's testable directly.

**How it resolves.** A variant is a tracked file whose name contains `##` plus comma-separated conditions on `hostname`, `os`, `arch`, or `profile`. All conditions must hold. When several match, the winner is the highest sum of condition weights (hostname 8 > profile 4 > arch 2 > os 1), so both a longer condition list and a stronger kind win. Ties break on file name, so the result never shifts between runs.

**Symlinks, not copies.** `~/.gitconfig` becomes a link to `.gitconfig##profile.work`. Verified: editing through the link modifies the variant, so `dotctl update` commits it normally and the repo never goes permanently dirty.

## Two judgment calls worth flagging

**A tracked plain path at a variant's target is a hard error, not forceable.** Linking over it would show the tracked file as permanently modified in git. `--force` replaces ordinary untracked files; it will not create that state. The error names the fix ("untrack it").

**`checkout` links variants automatically** (`--skip-profile` opts out) — that's the whole point of the "set up another computer" flow. But a conflict there is a warning, not a failure: checkout already succeeded, so exiting nonzero would misreport it. Standalone `profile apply` does fail loudly with a new `PROFILE_CONFLICT` code carrying `data.conflicts`.

Invalid variants (`##osx.darwin`) are reported with the list of valid kinds rather than silently skipped — a silently dropped variant is indistinguishable from one that didn't match, which is the worst possible failure mode here.

## Tests

Five, all guarding behavior that would be expensive to get wrong later: precedence ordering, tie determinism, invalid-variant reporting, refusing to clobber, refusing to replace a tracked target, and checkout integration including `--skip-profile`. Docs updated in `README.md` and the embedded `SKILL.md` (including a rule telling agents never to `--force` past the tracked-path conflict).

One thing I did not build: variant support for runnables. It's the obvious next step — `10-brew.sh##os.darwin` — but it's a separate feature and you picked one.
